subject: sewingMachine
pitch:
Category: Object.
Subject: treadle sewing machine.
Style: Victorian black and gold.
reasoning:
I'm thinking about whether this Victorian treadle sewing machine needs a rig at all—since it's a static prop, I could leave it joint-free, but adding a few simple joints for the wheel, treadle, and needle bar might give it more life while keeping the rig minimal with a single root joint.

I'm working out the real-world proportions: table roughly 0.9 x 0.45m with a 0.78m top height, cast-iron stand sides with scrolled feet, a treadle plate linked by a pitman rod to the flywheel, and deciding how the machine head and operator-facing side should be oriented in the scene.

That confirms the orientation, so now I'm laying out the treadle stand geometry: side frames at x=±0.36 with scrolled foot bars, tapered uprights, and a top bracket forming an openwork cast-iron silhouette extruded in the z-y plane.

Next I'm figuring the moving mechanism — a rocking treadle plate with openwork decal pattern, pivoted on side-frame screws, connected via a pitman rod to a flywheel crank at roughly (0.40, 0.32, 0) with radius 0.2, plus a thin belt loop running from the flywheel up to the machine's handwheel.

I'm working through the geometry of the belt path, deciding whether it should route through a slot in the table and placing the machine's small belt pulley near the head around x≈0.30 to connect realistically with the flywheel.

Simplifying the layout: table spans roughly ±0.45 in x, the machine body sits within that span, and the handwheel pulley and flywheel sit just beyond the head, positioned between the frame supports with the right radius and thickness so the belt and pitman crank connect properly.

I'll approximate the belts as simple round rods in dark brown, skipping the detailed wrap-around arcs on the flywheel for simplicity—good enough visually without overcomplicating the geometry.

Working out the arc direction via the rotation rule confirms it passes through the bottom as intended, and I apply similar logic for the pulley's belt wrap on the opposite side. Still computing geometry...

I should decide on joint hierarchy -- probably just root/base, flywheel, treadle, handwheel, and needleBar, assigning the belt to root so it doesn't get dragged by flywheel rotation, and specifying each joint's axis direction for part placement.

Now I'm sizing and positioning the main machine body on the table: a bed plate roughly 0.45-0.50m long and 0.17-0.18m wide, sitting at table height around 0.78m, with the needle end oriented toward -X.

Realizing the pillar should actually be at the +X end near the handwheel, with the arm extending left to the needle head, so I'm reworking the x-coordinates for the bed, pillar, and arm accordingly -- pillar around x=0.12 to 0.22, arm running from x=0.22 down to -0.24 at the height band above the bed.

I'm settling on total machine height around 1.1m, with the bed top at 0.805, arm clearance to 0.935, and the arm itself rising to 1.04, plus a spool pin on top near the pillar. Now I'm working out how to loft the arm shape using station profiles with width and height, following a curved path from the pillar to the head while keeping the orientation and widths aligned properly in world space.

I'm not sure loft accepts a sides parameter, so I'll just skip it and move to defining the paint—a glossy black japan finish with a subtle bluish sheen using a custom shader that mixes dark tones based on surface normal.

For the gold details, I'll pull brass/gilt materials from a clockwork kit and add Victorian-style gold decals with scrolling florals and serif text, naming the piece something fictional like "The Empress." I'm placing these decals on the front face of the arm (facing +Z) using the decal function targeting the loft geometry.

Writing SVG decal code...

For the remaining elements, I'm planning gold swirl banding on the bed plate, a treadle plate pattern, and considering an ebonised dark wood table with gold line accents to match the Victorian black-and-gold theme.

I'll place the drawer between -0.35 and -0.0 in black with a gold border decal and a gilt knob, plus spool pins holding thread—mostly cream and black, maybe one crimson accent for pop. Then I'll detail the needle area: the needle bar, presser bar and foot, thread take-up lever, brass tension discs, and a gold faceplate on the head, tracing the thread path with guides from spool to needle.

Next I'm handling the bed with a steel slide plate edged in gold and a bobbin cover, plus the needle plate near x=-0.2. For the handwheel at the +X end, I'm working out its radius and position with a black body and gold ring, a brass stop-motion knob, and making sure it doesn't collide with the belt wheel and arm geometry near x=0.25-0.33.

I'm figuring out where the belt groove sits on the handwheel's outer rim and tracing its path down to the flywheel, then checking whether it clears the pillar or needs a slot cut through the table — working out the slot's z-position and width so the belt can pass through unobstructed.

I need the treadle to fit within the frame width, so pitman and crank positions should sit around x≈0.31, with the flywheel radius of 0.2 centered around y=0.22 so its bottom clears the treadle space.

Thinking through the flywheel axle, I realize it should be mounted on the right frame rather than spanning fully between both frames, like a real treadle sewing machine stand. I'll place an axle running from x=0.25 to 0.40 with a bearing boss on the right frame, plus a small support bracket.

I'm mirroring the left frame at x=-0.39, with the table spanning ±0.45 and brackets with a 0.1-wide top plate supporting it. Now I'm laying out the frame's outline in the z-y plane as an extruded shape, designing the classic treadle-style silhouette.

Sketching leg outline coordinates...

Mapping out the mirrored left half completes the symmetric silhouette, but I realize a solid extruded plate won't capture the openwork look of a Victorian frame since extrusion can't easily create holes. I should instead construct the frame from separate pieces — a foot bar, columns, and top bracket — each extruded individually.

Designing the gold scrollwork decal...

Good, that confirms the right-direction symmetry works out fine either way.

Now I'm working out the treadle geometry — placing the rocking plate as a box roughly 0.60 by 0.025 by 0.25, pivoting on a rod along x near the front, with the plate extending backward from the pivot point.

Working out the pitman rod geometry connecting the treadle plate to the crank pin, matching lengths and angles so the linkage closes properly. Moving on to defining the treadle plate itself.

For the plate I'm thinking of a black box with an openwork diamond-lattice pattern overlaid using a gold decal texture facing upward, so the "VICTORIA" nameplate text reads correctly from the front. I need to orient the plane's up-vector properly so the texture isn't mirrored or rotated incorrectly when viewed from the standing position.

I also still need to add the treadle's heel-toe crossbar, pivot cone screws, and the tie rods bracing the two side frames — one near the top-back and a lower one at foot level — making sure they stay clear of the pitman and treadle's range of motion.

For the table, I'm planning the top as an ebonised wood box with a gold pinstripe border made from thin flush boxes near the edge, plus a moulded gold bead trim along the apron edges, with the sewing machine sitting on top. I'll skip a drop leaf for now and move toward finalizing the parts list, targeting somewhere between 180 and 340 components total.

I'm now sketching helper functions for boxes, cylinders, gold bands, hex-head bolts, and rivet rows, while trying to keep total part counts well under the limit. I need to be careful that joint-based bone assignment doesn't mistakenly attach static frame parts to moving joints like the flywheel, treadle, handwheel, or needle bar just because their bones pass nearby geometrically.

To fix that, I'll default static parts to explicit `bone: base`, using a mutable "current bone" variable that helpers reference automatically, which I can switch temporarily when building moving assemblies like the flywheel. I'll apply this same bone parameter consistently across sweeps, extrudes, lathes, lofts, and decals, and I'm now thinking through how the root joint and its children should be positioned starting from base at the origin.

I'm laying out the joint hierarchy: flywheel, treadle, handwheel, needleBar, and presserBar each get positions and directions relative to base, and the pitman rod attaches to the treadle bone since it's a moving link. I'm skipping the optional "role" attribute since this isn't a creature rig, and confirming the root joint can omit an explicit direction since it has no parent.

Now I'm shifting to the machine head itself, defining bed geometry constants like table-top height and bed extents, then planning to build the bed as an extruded rounded rectangle outline along the correct thickness axis, followed by lofting a pillar upward from the bed toward the arm.

I'm working out the pillar and arm as separate swept forms rather than one continuous loft, since direction changes make orientation ambiguous — settling on sweeping the pillar as an elliptical rod straight up, planning to join it to a curved horizontal arm with connecting spheres at the elbow.

Working out the arm cross-product gives either z-axis direction, so radial x maps to z and radial y maps to world y. Now I'm setting up the arm as a polyline sweep from the pillar at (0.17, 0.985, 0) over to (-0.19, 0.985, 0), tapering down toward a taller pillar-side profile.

Checking the tapered radii, the arm stays clear of the bed by about 0.11 units, and near the head end the ellipse narrows further before reaching a bulb with a bigger radius at x=-0.215. I'm adjusting the path's y-height slightly, from 0.985 to 0.99, so the arm reads as a gentle downward slant with rounded caps. For the head itself, I'm placing a vertical block containing the needle bar as a scaled sphere, then adding a faceplate disc that needs to face -X so it reads correctly from the +Z viewing angle.

I'm rethinking where the faceplate goes — on a real treadle Singer it sits at the left end of the head covering the needle bar mechanism, with the needle bar itself protruding at the bottom. Since the viewer sees the machine from +Z, I'll place a gilt faceplate disc on the -X end visible at a three-quarter angle, plus a smaller gold decorative roundel and decal on the arm's front face.

I'm positioning the needle bar near the head's underside around x=-0.225, running from the head bottom down to about y=0.85, with a brass clamp partway down and a thin needle tip extending further.

Now I'm placing the presser bar and foot slightly behind at x=-0.205, as a small wedge shape just above the throat plate, and defining the throat plate as a thin steel box sitting flush with the bed's top surface at y=0.81.

I'm also adding the bobbin cover slide plate with a gold-edged bright steel finish, a decorative gold scroll decal on the bed's top right, and the spool pin assembly at the arm top—a cylinder with a base boss and a lathed cream-and-brass thread spool.

Now I'm mapping out the thread path from spool to needle: positioning the wood spool with dark flanges and a tan or red thread core, then tracing guide points down through the tension assembly near the arm's head toward the needle area.

I'm placing the tension knob as a small brass knurled cylinder beside the head, then routing the thread through a take-up lever that sticks out from the head top with a small gold knob, before it drops down the needle bar to the needle eye.

I'm also adding a stitch-length regulator on the front of the pillar with a brass thumbscrew and gilt dial, and now I'm shaping the handwheel on the right side with a solid dished disc that has a V-shaped belt groove along its rim.

I'm adjusting the belt groove position to x=0.2675, checking it clears the elbow sphere and arm geometry which maxes around 0.245, so the handwheel can start cleanly at 0.255.

Now I'm detailing the handwheel assembly: a hidden shaft cylinder bridging the gap, a brass knurled stop-motion knob with a chrome cap further out, and a thin gold pinstripe ring decal on the wheel's face, with the wheel body painted black.

I'm also sketching a more elaborate flywheel design—a spoked cast iron wheel with a lathed rim profile, hub, eight tapered radiating spokes, and gold rim highlights, built using helper functions for closed circular paths and rod sweeps between hub and rim.

I'm thinking through visibility of the flywheel faces given the frame geometry — since the frame's right column sits in front of the flywheel center at certain z-ranges, part of the flywheel will be occluded while the gaps between the front and back legs should still reveal it from most viewing angles.

I want the flywheel to have a decorative face with black spokes accented by gold rim stripes and a gold hub, using tapered rod shapes for the spokes. I'm now working out the crank geometry — positioning the pin and rod connecting the hub to the crank arm, and reconsidering the flywheel's x-position so its belt groove aligns properly with the handwheel groove.

Now I'm laying out the drivetrain geometry along the x-axis: flywheel hub and groove, axle span between brackets, crank disc and pin, pitman arm connecting to the treadle, and the treadle plate extending outward on both sides to its pivot point against the frame's inner face.

I'll set the pivot rod along x at z=0.11, y=0.115 on the plate's underside, with pitman attachment near z=-0.12 and a short pitman-to-crank-pin length around 0.177. For the plate itself I'm sizing a base box roughly 0.66 wide by 0.30 deep, adding a raised rim border and an openwork golden lattice decal on top.

Underneath I'm adding diagonal ribs and a center hinge boss, while making sure the frame feet sit exactly at y=0 with a 0.03 extrusion thickness. I need a cross-tie rod connecting the frames at z=0, y≈0.55 — checking it threads between the flywheel and belt lines without collision — plus a top bracket flaring to ±0.22 in z at y=0.745 to support the table underside.

Now I'm laying out the table structure: apron rails along x on both sides, a drawer unit under the left half with a brass knob and gold decal front panel, and the tabletop itself split into left/right pieces with front and back strips framing a slot where the belt passes through.

For the tabletop finish, I'm applying an ebonized dark wood grain paint and adding thin gold inlay border lines inset around the perimeter, carefully positioned so they avoid the slot cutout, plus small gold fleur corner decals.

I'm now considering decorative touches for the legs—scroll feet with gold accent bands via decal planes on the frame faces. I'm sketching out an ornamental arm decal texture, planning its SVG layout to fit the tapered curve of the arm from pillar to tip.

Writing SVG scroll paths...

Mirroring the half-built shape to form the full symmetric design, then layering each stroke three times with a dark outline, gold fill, and thin highlight to create a gilded effect...

Now I'm adding the "EMPRESS" text in a cartouche with bold serif gold lettering and a dark outline, plus smaller "SEWING MACHINE" text and a decorative dot ribbon, along with spiral scroll shapes built from arc paths.

Writing leaf scroll paths...

Then I'm sketching T2 as a small vertical rosette decal with diamond petal pattern, and T3 as a flat scroll decal lying on the bed surface—using the decal helper projecting upward onto the bed's extruded part, which should also work for other flat faces like frames.

Next I'm placing T4 as a vertical acanthus stem decal on the frame's outer face, sized and positioned along its height, and sketching T5 as a horizontal scroll decal for the foot bar, working out its placement against the foot bar's thin tapered silhouette.

Then I'm planning T6 as a diamond lattice with a gold border for the treadle top, possibly bearing a name like "THE EMPRESS," followed by T8's fleur motif for table corners, T9's gold-bordered drawer front with a center ornament, and T10 as a possible gold stripe name plate along the bed's front edge.

Next I'm sketching T11 as a circular faceplate, built as a plane with a radial engraved texture at the end of the machine, plus T12 as a gauge dial showing numbers 0-5 in gold on black. I'm also considering adding a small bobbin winder wheel with a rubber ring on a bracket near the handwheel for extra detail.

Writing paint functions...

Now I'm defining the remaining materials: gilt and brass metals, steel, cast-iron reusing the japan paint, plus wood grain for the table, flat rubber black, leather belt brown, and thread colors in cream or crimson, keeping the overall flat-color palette limited.

I'm confirming textures and decals stay within the lighting setup without needing glow effects, then sketching the imports I'll need from the builder library and clockwork kit, settling on just the metal helper plus the core drawing primitives.

Skipping the gear train since it won't be visible, and double-checking which utilities like DEG, mix, noise are exported from the math and paint modules. I'm setting up the build function with metadata and initializing the builder and random seed for the treadle sewing machine model.

Now I'm defining the base joint and bone tracking variable, then sketching helper functions for creating box geometry parts with color and transform options, working out the right types for colors and part parameters based on the builder's overloads.

I'm settling on using loose `any` typing for the options objects to keep things flexible without fighting TypeScript, then writing a cylinder helper that wraps `CylinderGeometry` with configurable radii, segments, and direction vectors.

Now I'm adding more helper functions: a sphere/ball builder, a rod connector between two points, a hex bolt generator using a 6-sided cylinder, and a function to compute ring paths around circles using an aim-based basis for orientation.

Good, closed paths sweep cleanly with no caps or seam. Now I'm building the frame geometry for both sides by extruding the frame outline profile along each side, with bevel and smoothing for a rounded edge.

I need to check if smoothing level 1 could cause problems on sharp corners or short edges in the outline — particularly near the narrow column section where quarter-length cuts might cross other edges given how tight some of those segments are, like the ones around 0.04,0.22 and 0.035,0.5.

Checking those remaining corner candidates for crossing cuts — they look fine with smoothing 1. For the extrude mapping, the u/v axes correspond to z and y, so sign doesn't matter since the shape is symmetric anyway. I'm thinking the solid silhouette could use some visual interest, so I'll add gold C-scroll decorative sweeps on top as openwork detailing.

Now I want to add spiral curl decals at each foot end for a Victorian flourish, plus a raised gold bead sweeping along the outline edge on both faces to outline the silhouette — using an inset polyline of the raw outline points for that bead path.

Writing polygon inset math...

I'll use a closed polyline with small round caps rather than catmull smoothing, since overshoot risk isn't worth the smoothness gain here. The bead should sit inside the slightly rounded inner corners after insetting, which should look fine even with minor discrepancies, and I'll need four sweeps total (outer and inner per side) for the dark body.

Now checking the frame geometry: the top cap flange looks right, but I'm second-guessing the bearing boss placement at the flywheel axle and the treadle pivot bosses, since the pivot point at y=0.115, z=0.11 seems to fall just outside the foot's silhouette based on the edge interpolation between the two polygon points there — I need to adjust the pivot position to actually sit within the foot shape.

I'll reposition the treadle pivot to z=0 at y=0.13, centered on the frame column where the width comfortably fits, making it a rocker-style pivot rather than offset toward either edge. I'm also sketching in cone pivot screws connecting the frame's inner face to the treadle plate's end boss, and starting to work out the flywheel axle geometry.

Now I'm figuring out how to support the inner axle end: a bracket or hanger pair dropping from the table underside, positioned just inside the table's slot edge so it doesn't interfere with the belt path, with a flange detail still needing work.

Checking that this strut clears the flywheel's position along x, confirming they don't collide. Then I'm setting up the flywheel's joint position and orientation on the x-axis, and starting to lay out six spokes radiating around it at even angular intervals.

Adding spoke and hub geometry...

Pitman pin P attaches to treadle attach point T, mounted on the bottom end of the treadle bone with a gold ring at the pin. I'm working out the treadle plate's position—extending ±0.335 in x, with the pitman attaching near its top edge—and figuring out where the pivot rod needs to pass relative to the plate.

Trying to settle the pivot rod's exact height so it sits under the plate without intersecting it, while also checking the frame column width at that height to ensure clearance. I also need to verify the plate's z-extent doesn't collide with the frame's foot near the base.

Now I'm checking the table dimensions against the frame top brackets and feet, making sure the table surface, machine bed, and handwheel don't overlap the sewing table's slot or supports.

I'm tracing the belt path from the handwheel groove down to the flywheel groove, computing tangent points and checking the belt clears the table slot edge at y=0.78 — it comes out to about 0.095, safely inside the 0.12 slot boundary.

Now I'm verifying the arc directions for the belt loops: checking that the top arc over the handwheel rotates correctly from z=-0.058 up over the top to z=+0.058 using a rotation about the x-axis, confirming it passes through +y at the midpoint as expected for wrapping over the top of the pulley. Then I'm setting up the corresponding bottom arc for the flywheel side.

I'm defining the belt as a swept tube with a small radius and pentagonal cross-section, colored dark leather, treated as a fixed static piece since nothing moves it. Moving on to defining the arm and head geometry, I'm setting up height constants for the table top, bed top, and arm centre, then starting to extrude the bed's plan outline along the x and z directions.

Still writing bed outline coordinates...

Tweaking elbow sphere scale to match arm proportions, then defining the arm sweep path with a tapering radius function along two points.

Now I'm working out the head geometry -- sizing the bulb sphere and positioning it against the arm's end point, then figuring out where the needle should emerge from the bottom of the head to stay within the bulb's footprint.

Positioning the gilt faceplate boss and textured disc against the sphere's curved surface...

For the texture itself, I'm designing a gold gradient circular plate with concentric engraved rings and a vertical take-up slot in black for the winding mechanism, plus a tiny lever rod protruding from the slot with a small ball tip.

Now I'm positioning the needle bar mechanism: a bone joint driving a thin brass bar down through a clamp cylinder to the needle tip, checking that it clears the throat plate properly. I'm also working out where to place the static presser bar relative to the needle's x-position so the head geometry doesn't collide.

I'm placing the presser bar slightly to the side of the needle, with a shank connecting down to a foot plate that extends toward the needle with a slot, and adding a knurled brass thumbscrew cap at the top of the head.

I'll simplify the presser foot geometry to two toe boxes positioned symmetrically along the z-axis, with a slot between them for the needle, rather than trying to replicate exact real-world foot orientation.

Then I'm adding the throat plate as a steel box with feed dog grooves and dark slots for detail, and a bed slide plate positioned alongside it to complete the needle-area hardware.

Next I'm placing a stitch regulator dial on the pillar front — a small cylinder with a textured circle face, positioned to align with the pillar's curved surface.

Positioning the texture circle slightly above the dial face along its normal, computing the offset using the embed depth so it sits just above the pillar surface without clipping.

Thinking through placement for the pillar decal and dial decal so they don't overlap near the elbow joint, adjusting their y-coordinates to separate them along the pillar's 0.80-0.96 range.

Working out the arm decal placement next...

Now I'm working out the gilt pinstripe angle convention along the arm's sweep direction, figuring out how the clock-style angle (0 up, 90 clockwise) maps through rotation about the −X travel axis, so that +90° correctly lands on the correct side of the tube rather than the mirrored one.

I'll sidestep the orientation ambiguity by just placing symmetric decorative lines at four angles (50°, 310°, 130°, 230°) using thin gilt sweep lines with small radius and lift, keeping the design visually symmetric regardless of exact front/back labeling.

For the bed edge pinstripes, I'm checking that the bed outline polygon winds counterclockwise in (x,z) space so my inset function, which assumes CCW ordering, produces a correctly inward-offset gold stripe along the bed's border.

Now I'm shifting to the table piece, defining its wood grain texture and adding thin gold accent lines inset from the table top edge.

Adding gilt edge rods now, then building the drawer: a front panel, a bottom casing box, and side panels to frame it under the tabletop.

Checking that the casing sides clear the frame, I'm adding apron rails at front and back to connect the leg frames, plus a cross tie rod positioned below the drawer to brace the structure.

Adding more hardware: bolt heads securing the stretcher to the frame, a brass ID badge decal on the column, and figuring out the spool pin position by calculating the arm's curve height at a specific point along its taper.

Working out the spool shape as a lathe profile with flanges and a core, plus a separate cream-colored thread cylinder sitting on top.

Now I'm positioning the spool pin on the arm's flat top at z=0, and considering whether to add a second pin as a bobbin winder plus a small thread guide, then starting to trace the thread path from the spool.

I'm placing a small bent-wire thread guide loop above the arm top, then locating the tension disc assembly on the front face of the head near the head's upper-left area, matching where Singer machines typically put the tension dial.

Now I'm tracing the full thread path from spool through the guide wire, down across the arm, and finally into the tension dial mechanism.

I'm checking that each thread point clears the head's curved surface by computing the sphere radius at different heights, then continuing the path outward to the lever eye near x=-0.27, y=1.0.

Writing coordinate list for the needle path...

Checking other points against arm geometry confirms they clear the surface, and the tension dial position looks far enough from the thread path to avoid collision. I'll keep the thread thin with a small radius and minimal sides, using a red color for visibility against the machine's black/gold body, with the thread end attaching near the needle bar. For the bobbin winder, I'm placing it on the front side of the arm near the top of the pillar.

Rather than overthinking precise placement, I'll just settle on a spot at the top of the arm, slightly offset from the spool pin and handwheel to avoid crowding, and move forward since the part count target (~250) means I need to keep adding bolts, rivets, and other small details rather than dwelling on this one piece.

I'll skip a full winder mechanism and instead attach a small tire-like ring disc to the handwheel shaft for a minimal touch. For oiling points, I'm adding small brass oil-hole covers as tiny gold cylinders scattered across the arm top and head, placed near the top surface at steep elevation angles. I'll also add rivets and screw heads along the arm sides, plus gilt pinstripe detailing on the flywheel rim faces at two slightly offset radial positions.

Now I'm working out the flywheel rim geometry with circular sweep paths on both faces, considering frame cast details like inner/outer beads, gilt acorn finials on the top corners of the flange, and spiral gold volute scrolls decorating the ends of the base feet.

Still working out spiral positions...

Now I'm defining a gilded-stroke helper that layers a darker outline beneath a lighter gold path to give the engraving a raised, metallic look.

Still designing arm texture paths...

Still writing SVG decoration...

Still writing SVG texture code...

Now I'm checking the bed-top decal layout, making sure the pillar base and slide plate regions don't overlap and figuring out the free space left for the small monogram decal between them.

Still writing decal patterns...

For a column decoration, I'm sketching a vertical gilded spine with alternating mirrored C-scroll leaves running along its length and ring details capping the ends, then checking the texture ratio and decal sizing so the column proportions fit within the taper from top to bottom.

Now I'm laying out the foot strip texture as a scrolling wave motif with dots, sized and positioned to work around the column's footprint, and designing a lattice texture for the treadle top with a gilded rounded border, diagonal diamond lattice lines with small circles at the crossings, and a central cartouche reading "THE EMPRESS."

Still designing textures...

For gold plate details I'm adding radial gradient fill, rings, screws, and a slot. The handwheel can skip texture detail, just lathe black with a gold ring sweep.

For applying these as decals onto parts like the drawer or treadle top, I'm planning a helper function that creates a textured plane positioned and oriented against a bone, using a simple part-creation call with the decal texture applied.

For the frame and curved arm decals, I'm working out exact positions and sizes so the plane sits flush against the surface with proper orientation, using the decal helper against the sweep geometry.

Setting up imports and starting the build script...

Now I'm defining the materials palette—gilt, brass, steel, iron, japan paint, wood grain—and thinking through texel density for the painted sheets based on total painted surface area across the model.

I'm bumping the paint resolution to 2048 for sharper detail while staying within the atlas limit. To avoid generating too many separate charts for tiny parts like bolts, I'll switch those to flat color swatches instead of full paint, keeping the total color count low. Now I'm writing the procedural japan paint shader function...

Writing polygon inset function...

Defining frame polygon coordinates...

Checking edge lengths near the top corners look fine, and verifying the foot height isn't too thin along the z-axis.

Now I'm computing the inset bead points along the frame polyline and checking miter joints at sharp vertices for correctness. I also need to adjust the bead's sweep offset slightly so it sits properly embedded against the beveled front face rather than floating or clipping.

With the frame geometry settled, I'm moving to organize the overall build order: imports and constants, the builder setup with joints, then frames, treadle/flywheel/belt, table and drawer, and finally assembling the machine. I'm now defining the joint hierarchy for the base, flywheel, treadle, handwheel, and needle positions...

Defining joint hierarchy...

Defining the gold ring helper and color constants...

More hex colors and a bolt helper for hardware, then I'm starting the frame geometry loop that builds both sides symmetrically.

Closed polylines just get no caps since there's no open seam, which makes sense here. Now adding decals for the column and foot textures, positioned on the outer face with sizes matching the panel dimensions, then checking the foot strip's silhouette against the panel's curved top edge.

Writing volute spiral code...

I should set pitch to 0 explicitly for a flat coil, and I'm checking that the volute position at z=±0.215 with radius 0.018 fits within the foot's height profile without clashing with the decal strip.

Placing bolt heads along the outer face of the flange where it spans z up to 0.225, plus a couple more on the foot. For the pivot cone screws, I'm positioning tapered cylinders from the inner face angled toward center, oriented so the tip points inward.

Adding more parts...

For the right frame's axle bearing, I'm setting a brass boss at the inner face with a matching gold cap bolt outside, then running the axle itself across with a flywheel rotating on it -- leaving the left side bare. Now adding a tie rod spanning from one side to the other at the upper frame height.

I'm placing another cross rod near the top back under the flange area, then adding a wooden stretcher rail beneath the table, followed by the front rail sections positioned to clear the belt path. Now I'm starting the treadle assembly with its main plate.

Adding raised border edges and the pivot rod...

Adding the pitman rod geometry with gold accent rings at both connection ends for visual contrast against the dark steel finish.

Now I'm building the flywheel assembly: a lathed rim with a bone-colored japan finish, a cylindrical hub with a gold cap, and spoke placeholders connecting them radially.

Adding gold trim rings on the rim faces, then working out the crank assembly—disc, gold ring plate, and a pin offset within the disc radius so it can connect to the pitman rod while rotating with the flywheel.

Now I'm laying out the belt and table geometry: breaking the tabletop into boxes by region (A through D) with specific widths and depths in wood, setting the base in bone material, and planning gold inlay lines along the top edges.

Working through the border lines crossing C and D at the correct z-depths, adding vertical border lines, and placing small gold rosettes at the corners to cover the line intersections, sitting on a slightly elevated decal plane. I'm also figuring out the rosette texture as a cut-out gold circle on a transparent plane, then moving to the edge gold beading as small rods.
